overview.text: The liver is the largest gland in the body, weighing about three pounds in an adult.
overview.label: 23.6 The Liver

overview.text: The liver lies inferior to the diaphragm in the right upper quadrant of the abdominal cavity and receives protection from the surrounding ribs.
overview.label: 23.6 The Liver

overview.text: The liver is divided into two primary lobes: a large right lobe and a much smaller left lobe.
overview.label: 23.6 The Liver

overview.text: In the right lobe, some anatomists also identify an inferior quadrate lobe and a posterior caudate lobe, which are defined by internal features.
overview.label: 23.6 The Liver

overview.text: The porta hepatis (“gate to the liver”) is where the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein enter the liver.
overview.label: 23.6 The Liver

lobes.text: The liver is divided into two primary lobes: a large right lobe and a much smaller left lobe.
lobes.label: 23.6 The Liver

lobes.text: In the right lobe, some anatomists also identify an inferior quadrate lobe and a posterior caudate lobe, which are defined by internal features.
lobes.label: 23.6 The Liver

portal.text: The porta hepatis (“gate to the liver”) is where the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein enter the liver.
portal.label: 23.6 The Liver

portal.text: The hepatic portal vein delivers partially deoxygenated blood containing nutrients absorbed from the small intestine and actually supplies more oxygen to the liver than do the much smaller hepatic arteries.
portal.label: 23.6 The Liver

portal.text: With this hepatic portal circulation, all blood from the alimentary canal passes through the liver.
portal.label: 23.6 The Liver

arteries.text: The porta hepatis (“gate to the liver”) is where the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein enter the liver.
arteries.label: 23.6 The Liver

arteries.text: A hepatic sinusoid is an open, porous blood space formed by fenestrated capillaries from nutrient-rich hepatic portal veins and oxygen-rich hepatic arteries.
arteries.label: 23.6 Histology

hveins.text: After processing the bloodborne nutrients and toxins, the liver releases nutrients needed by other cells back into the blood, which drains into the central vein and then through the hepatic vein to the inferior vena cava.
hveins.label: 23.6 The Liver

hveins.text: Blood then flows through a hepatic vein into the inferior vena cava.
hveins.label: 23.6 Histology

biliary.text: The bile ducts unite to form the larger right and left hepatic ducts, which themselves merge and exit the liver as the common hepatic duct.
biliary.label: 23.6 Histology

biliary.text: This duct then joins with the cystic duct from the gallbladder, forming the common bile duct through which bile flows into the small intestine.
biliary.label: 23.6 Histology

cystic.text: The cystic duct is 1–2 cm (less than 1 in) long and turns inferiorly as it bridges the neck and hepatic duct.
cystic.label: 23.6 The Gallbladder

cystic.text: This duct then joins with the cystic duct from the gallbladder, forming the common bile duct through which bile flows into the small intestine.
cystic.label: 23.6 Histology

gallbladder.text: The gallbladder is 8–10 cm (~3–4 in) long and is nested in a shallow area on the posterior aspect of the right lobe of the liver.
gallbladder.label: 23.6 The Gallbladder

gallbladder.text: This muscular sac stores, concentrates, and, when stimulated, propels the bile into the duodenum via the common bile duct.
gallbladder.label: 23.6 The Gallbladder

gallbladder.text: It is divided into three regions.
gallbladder.label: 23.6 The Gallbladder

gallbladder.text: The fundus is the widest portion and tapers medially into the body, which in turn narrows to become the neck.
gallbladder.label: 23.6 The Gallbladder

pancreas.text: The soft, oblong, glandular pancreas lies transversely in the retroperitoneum behind the stomach.
pancreas.label: 23.6 The Pancreas

pancreas.text: Its head is nestled into the “c-shaped” curvature of the duodenum with the body extending to the left about 15.2 cm (6 in) and ending as a tapering tail in the hilum of the spleen.
pancreas.label: 23.6 The Pancreas

pducts.text: These acinar cells secrete enzyme-rich pancreatic juice into tiny merging ducts that form two dominant ducts.
pducts.label: 23.6 The Pancreas

pducts.text: The larger duct fuses with the common bile duct (carrying bile from the liver and gallbladder) just before entering the duodenum via a common opening (the hepatopancreatic ampulla).
pducts.label: 23.6 The Pancreas

pducts.text: The second and smaller pancreatic duct, the accessory duct (duct of Santorini), runs from the pancreas directly into the duodenum, approximately 1 inch above the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
pducts.label: 23.6 The Pancreas

duodenum.text: The shortest region is the 25.4-cm (10-in) duodenum, which begins at the pyloric sphincter.
duodenum.label: 23.5 Structure

duodenum.text: Just past the pyloric sphincter, it bends posteriorly behind the peritoneum, becoming retroperitoneal, and then makes a C-shaped curve around the head of the pancreas before ascending anteriorly again to return to the peritoneal cavity and join the jejunum.
duodenum.label: 23.5 Structure

ivc.text: Blood then flows through a hepatic vein into the inferior vena cava.
ivc.label: 23.6 Histology
